full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN.** This is the (N=6, r=3) cyclic predator-prey system, which the literature calls a six-species coarsening system with spirals inside the domains. I'm highly confident about the qualitative behaviour. I'm less sure about the exact numerical thresholds.

**1. Model family.** This is a stochastic spatial multispecies Lotka–Volterra / May–Leonard system, studied as cyclic dominance in evolutionary game theory and statistical physics. The notation (N, r) means N species, each preying cyclically on r others. Here each species eats the next three, so this is (6,3). Because site occupancy is unrestricted and individuals hop between sites, it is a bosonic or metapopulation implementation.

**2. Where the behaviour is described.**
- **Two alliances.** Species i and i+3 eat each other, so the odd species {1,3,5} and the even species {2,4,6} each form a three-species rock-paper-scissors loop. Within each loop, species do not fight members of the other loop's alliance except across interfaces.
  - The coarsening papers describe domains each holding a team (1,3,5) or (2,4,6) with cyclic interactions. Each domain contains a team of three species, either (1,3,5) or (2,4,6), with cyclic interactions.
  - Roman, Dasgupta & Pleimling (2013) report the same pattern. One observes coarsening domains with non-trivial spirals forming inside the domains.
  - They find that the domains grow algebraically. Even when alliance members are themselves in a predator-prey relationship, domain growth follows L(t) ~ t^{1/2}.
- **Two territories, three species each, spirals inside.** The Dobramysl–Mobilia–Pleimling–Täuber review (2018) describes the (6,3) case as two coarsening domain types with a non-trivial rock-paper-scissors game within the domains.
  - The review also covers the unrestricted-occupancy case. The spirals-within-domains pattern was first found with at most one individual per site, but is also seen in a bosonic implementation without a hard occupation limit. That matches the many-individuals-per-site rules here.
- **Eating-to-crowding ratio thresholds.** The papers vary the rate ratios, but I found no source stating the specific thresholds (split at 1, chasing at 2).
  - Esmaeili, Brown & Pleimling studied changing the predation and reproduction rates in the (6,3) model, and they report similar quantitative changes to the in-domain space-time patterns when changing the rates.
  - In the three-species case, the Hopf-type threshold for spiral formation is a standard result in the review by Täuber and co-authors (arXiv 2405.05006).
  - The numerical values 1 and 2 are probably specific to this rule set's rate definitions, and I could not check them against the literature.
- **Long-time single territory.** The coarsening literature predicts that domains keep growing. On a finite periodic lattice, one team would eventually take over. I didn't find a paper that states this outcome explicitly for (6,3).
- **Related variants.**
  - The Avelino et al. even-N papers (including N=6) describe two partnerships, {1,3,5} and {2,4,6}, forming separate domains. There are two partnerships, {1,3,5} and {2,4,6}, each occupying separate spatial regions on the lattice.
  - Szabó, Szolnoki & Sznaider (2008) treat even n=4, 6, 8, where two defective alliances form, made up of the even and odd label species.

**Earliest clear sources and a review.**
- Earliest: Roman, Dasgupta & Pleimling, "Interplay between partnership formation and competition in generalized May-Leonard games", Phys. Rev. E 87, 032148 (2013), arXiv 1303.3139.
  - I checked the title and authors against the arXiv result and reference lists.
  - The PRE volume and page come from a citing paper's reference list.
  - Related earlier work: Szabó, Szolnoki & Sznaider, "Segregation process and phase transition in cyclic predator-prey models with even number of species" (arXiv 0710.3371, 2007; Phys. Rev. E 77, 011906 (2008)).
  - The PRE 77 volume and page are from memory, not from the search results.
- In-depth study: Brown & Pleimling et al., "Coarsening with non-trivial in-domain dynamics: correlations and interface fluctuations" (arXiv 1707.03447).
  - I confirmed the title and arXiv number.
  - I did not confirm the exact author list or venue from the results, so I leave it out of the citation.
- Perturbation study: Esmaeili, Brown & Pleimling, Phys. Rev. E 98, 062105 (2018).
- Review: Dobramysl, Mobilia, Pleimling & Täuber, "Stochastic population dynamics in spatially extended predator-prey systems", arXiv 1708.07055, published in J. Phys. A (2018).
  - I confirmed the title and arXiv number. I did not confirm the authors from the results; the venue, the author list and the 2018 date are from memory.
  - The general cyclic-dominance review is Szolnoki et al., J. R. Soc. Interface 11, 20140735 (2014).

**3. Searches run:**
- Six species with each eating three, two sub-communities, rock-paper-scissors.
- Szolnoki cyclic dominance review.
- Generalized rock-paper-scissors N species with Avelino, coarsening and sub-networks.
- The Esmaeili et al. title.
- Patterns within patterns, six-species, spirals within coarsening domains.
- Roman et al. (6,3), predation versus reproduction rate dependence.

**4. Confidence: high for the qualitative behaviour, medium for the numbers.** Multiple independent groups and a review describe the two three-species territories with spirals inside, and the unrestricted-occupancy version is explicitly noted. The 1D ring variants with hop rates 0.1 and 1 were not searched separately. They fall in the same (6,3) family, but in 1D spirals cannot form, so only the alliance and domain behaviour should carry over.
